pregameSituation.title: Shivam Medical Store
pregameSituation.text:
Shivam Medical Store has been buying all its stock of a common fever/flu medicine from one regular supplier for years. The supplier offers good pricing, reliable deliveries, and a trusted relationship with Shivam.

Suddenly, a viral outbreak hits the city. Demand for this medicine triples overnight, and panic-buying begins.

The regular supplier cannot keep up. They are rationing supply across all their retail clients and cannot provide Shivam with additional stock immediately.

A new supplier appears, offering to fulfil the full additional demand immediately — but at a higher price and with no prior relationship or track record.

If Shivam uses the new supplier, the regular supplier may perceive it as disloyalty and potentially deprioritize Shivam once the crisis ends and supply normalizes.

If Shivam stays loyal and waits, shelves remain empty during the outbreak. Customers may shift to competing pharmacies and may not return.

Shivam must decide how to manage its supply chain during the crisis.

questions.title: The First Call
questions.situation: The regular supplier says no extra stock is available. The new supplier can deliver the full quantity needed, but Shivam has never worked with them before.
questions.optionA: Place a trial order with the new supplier for a limited quantity to test their reliability while assessing the situation.
questions.optionB: Commit fully to the new supplier for the entire required quantity to guarantee availability during the crisis.
questions.explanation: Committing fully to an unverified supplier exposes Shivam to quality and reliability risk it has no way to check yet. A trial order tests the new relationship without betting the whole crisis response on an unknown.
questions.consequence: The trial batch arrives on time and in good condition — Shivam must now decide whether to scale up.

questions.title: Scaling Up
questions.situation: The trial batch arrived on time and was good quality. The outbreak is still growing.
questions.optionA: Place a large follow-up order with the new supplier now, to lock in supply before prices rise further.
questions.optionB: Place a moderate follow-up order and reassess again in a few days as demand data comes in.
questions.explanation: Outbreak-driven demand is inherently uncertain — it could keep rising or could peak and fall quickly. A large commitment now risks expensive, short-shelf-life overstock if demand drops. A moderate order preserves flexibility.
questions.consequence: A moderate order is placed. The regular supplier unexpectedly calls back.

questions.title: The Regular Supplier Calls Back
questions.situation: The regular supplier offers a small quantity at the old, lower price — a loyalty gesture. But accepting it means juggling two supply lines during a chaotic week.
questions.optionA: Accept the regular supplier's offer to preserve the long-term relationship, even if it adds coordination complexity.
questions.optionB: Politely decline for now and stick with the new supplier's committed schedule to avoid confusing supply lines.
questions.explanation: A small order is easy to absorb operationally, and it keeps a valuable long-term relationship alive. Running two suppliers in parallel (dual sourcing) also reduces Shivam's dependence on the untested new supplier.
questions.consequence: Shivam now has stock flowing from both suppliers — at different prices. Cash is getting tight.

questions.title: The Cash Squeeze
questions.situation: Between the two suppliers, this week's spending on the flu medicine is eating into the cash Shivam needs for other essential stock and running costs.
questions.optionA: Use most of the available cash on the flu medicine, since it's the most urgent need right now.
questions.optionB: Cap spending on the flu medicine and preserve a cash buffer for other essential stock and expenses.
questions.explanation: Over-committing working capital to one fast-moving item risks stockouts elsewhere and a cash crunch — total cost thinking means looking beyond this one product line, not just this one crisis.
questions.consequence: Spend is capped, so total stock is still short of full demand. Someone has to be served first.

questions.title: Who Gets the Limited Stock?
questions.situation: Combined stock still can't cover total demand. Regular customers, new walk-ins, and the hospital all want it.
questions.optionA: Sell strictly first-come, first-served to everyone.
questions.optionB: Reserve a portion for regular, long-standing customers and prescriptions, and sell the rest first-come.
questions.explanation: Core customer segmentation — focusing service on the most valuable, long-term relationships — is a standard inventory deployment principle. It protects the customer base Shivam depends on beyond the crisis.
questions.consequence: Regular customers are prioritized. Word spreads that Shivam has stock, and walk-in demand climbs further.

questions.title: Forecasting the Next Order
questions.situation: Sales data shows demand has tripled. A local news report hints the outbreak might peak within a week — but this isn't confirmed.
questions.optionA: Base the next order on the actual current spike in sales.
questions.optionB: Base the next order on a moderated forecast — blending the pre-outbreak average with the recent spike.
questions.explanation: Ordering purely off the latest spike is a classic forecasting trap — it overreacts to a temporary signal and sets up a bigger correction (and possible bullwhip effect) later if the spike doesn't hold.
questions.consequence: A moderate order goes out. Stock is still tight enough that safety stock policy needs a decision.

questions.title: The Safety Stock Question
questions.situation: Demand has proven volatile and hard to predict. Shivam considers whether to raise safety stock for this item.
questions.optionA: Increase safety stock moderately, even though it ties up more capital and shelf space.
questions.optionB: Keep safety stock modest and instead lean on faster supplier response for future spikes.
questions.explanation: This is a cost-of-waiting vs. cost-of-preparedness call. A stockout here doesn't just lose a sale — it risks losing the hospital relationship worth much more. Given that risk, the modest extra holding cost is clearly justified.
questions.concept: Safety stock / cost of preparedness vs. cost of waiting
questions.consequence: Extra stock is held. The new supplier requests something in return.

questions.title: The Data Request
questions.situation: The new supplier asks Shivam to share its actual daily sales data so they can plan allocation more accurately for Shivam specifically.
questions.optionA: Share the sales data to help the supplier serve Shivam more accurately and build a prioritized relationship.
questions.optionB: Decline to share detailed data, keeping information private to retain negotiating flexibility.
questions.explanation: Poor information flow is one of the biggest drivers of supply chain distortion (the bullwhip effect). Sharing real demand data helps the supplier allocate correctly instead of guessing — which benefits Shivam directly.
questions.consequence: Allocation improves. But a different information problem appears — this time from the hospital.

questions.title: The Hospital's Panic Order
questions.situation: The hospital, worried about future shortages, places an order far larger than its normal usage — stockpiling.
questions.optionA: Fulfil the hospital's full stockpiling order, since they are a major customer.
questions.optionB: Fulfil part of the order now and encourage the hospital to place smaller, more frequent orders based on actual usage.
questions.explanation: Large, fear-driven batch orders are a textbook bullwhip-effect trigger — they distort the real demand signal and can cause overstock or shortages later. Smoothing the order size keeps the signal honest.
questions.consequence: The hospital agrees to smaller orders. Supply is stabilizing — attention turns to how reorders are triggered.

questions.title: Setting the Reorder Trigger
questions.situation: With better information now flowing in, Shivam must decide how future reorders for this item get triggered.
questions.optionA: Set a fixed reorder point based on pre-crisis average demand, for simplicity.
questions.optionB: Set a reorder point that adjusts based on recent actual sales trends.
questions.explanation: A fixed, pre-crisis reorder point ignores everything just learned about this item's volatility. A responsive reorder mechanism matches actual conditions rather than an outdated average.
questions.consequence: The supply flow stabilizes. Physical stock from both suppliers is now sitting in the store — with different expiry dates.

questions.title: Two Batches, Two Expiry Dates
questions.situation: The new supplier's batch has a shorter remaining shelf life than the regular supplier's batch. Both are currently in stock.
questions.optionA: Shelve and sell the shorter-expiry batch first, keeping the longer-expiry batch behind it.
questions.optionB: Mix both batches together on the shelf for simplicity during the rush, since both are within date.
questions.explanation: This is FEFO (First-Expired-First-Out) — standard practice for shelf-life-sensitive products. Mixing batches risks the longer-dated stock being sold first and the shorter-dated batch expiring unsold.
questions.consequence: Staff are stretched thin during the rush. The extra stock volume itself becomes a storage problem.

questions.title: Running Out of Shelf Space
questions.situation: Combined emergency stock from two suppliers now exceeds Shivam's usual storage space.
questions.optionA: Rent short-term extra storage space nearby to keep stock organized and accessible.
questions.optionB: Stack overflow stock wherever space allows in the store, accepting some disorganization temporarily.
questions.explanation: Disorganized stacking directly undermines FEFO and materials handling — batches get buried, mixed up, or damaged, risking exactly the wastage the extra stock was meant to prevent. The short-term rental cost is small next to that risk.
questions.consequence: Extra space is arranged. Now a routine replenishment decision comes up.

questions.title: Choosing a Delivery Option
questions.situation: The new supplier offers a slower, cheaper consolidated delivery (shared with other pharmacies) or a costlier dedicated express delivery.
questions.optionA: Use the shared consolidated delivery to reduce transportation cost per unit.
questions.optionB: Pay for dedicated express delivery to eliminate any delay risk during the ongoing crisis.
questions.explanation: With safety stock already raised and reorder points now responsive, the stockout risk this delivery is protecting against is already covered. Premium transport should be reserved for genuine emergencies, not routine restocking.
questions.consequence: Costs stabilize. A competitor makes a move.

questions.title: The Competitor Undercuts
questions.situation: A rival pharmacy starts selling the same medicine at a lower price, having found a cheaper distributor.
questions.optionA: Match the competitor's lower price to retain footfall, accepting a thinner margin.
questions.optionB: Hold the current price, leaning on Shivam's proven reliability and availability during the shortage.
questions.explanation: Shivam has just built a real differentiator — it stayed stocked when others didn't. Cutting price now erodes the margin needed to cover higher emergency procurement costs, for a battle that isn't really about price.
questions.consequence: Price holds. A loyal customer questions why the price hasn't come down.

questions.title: A Customer Pushes Back on Price
questions.situation: A regular customer notices the price is unchanged from before the crisis and feels it should be lower, unaware procurement costs actually rose.
questions.optionA: Explain transparently that procurement costs rose due to emergency sourcing.
questions.optionB: Avoid the topic and simply reassure the customer that the pricing is fair.
questions.explanation: This is customer-facing communication, not competitive negotiation — the caution about protecting information applied to a rival supplier, not a loyal customer. Transparency here builds the trust that Shivam is relying on as its differentiator.
questions.consequence: The customer accepts the explanation. Meanwhile, the outbreak itself is starting to shift.

questions.title: Early Signs of a Peak
questions.situation: News suggests the outbreak may be peaking, but there's no confirmed data yet.
questions.optionA: Start reducing order sizes now, anticipating the fall in demand.
questions.optionB: Continue current order levels a little longer until there's clearer confirmation of a decline.
questions.explanation: Acting on an unconfirmed signal risks a repeat stockout if the outbreak continues — the same overreaction trap as before, just in the opposite direction. Wait for the trend to actually confirm itself.
questions.consequence: Orders hold steady. The regular supplier's situation is also changing.

questions.title: The Regular Supplier Eases Rationing
questions.situation: The regular supplier can now offer a moderate ongoing quantity again, alongside what the new supplier provides.
questions.optionA: Gradually shift back to the regular supplier as the primary source, now that normalcy is returning.
questions.optionB: Continue splitting orders between both suppliers to maintain flexibility.
questions.explanation: This crisis specifically exposed the risk of relying on one supplier. Reverting immediately throws away a resilience lesson that was expensive to learn — splitting orders keeps that protection in place.
questions.concept: Supply chain resilience / single vs. multiple sourcing
questions.consequence: Dual sourcing continues. Meanwhile, actual demand starts to turn.

questions.title: Demand Starts Falling
questions.situation: Confirmed reports now show the outbreak declining. Sales of the flu medicine are dropping toward normal, and current stock levels look like they may become excess.
questions.optionA: Slow down future orders immediately and sell down existing stock through normal channels.
questions.optionB: Offer a limited-time discount right away to accelerate sales of existing stock before it approaches expiry.
questions.explanation: The first lever against a demand slowdown is to stop making the excess worse — cut future ordering. Discounting immediately sacrifices margin before it's actually needed; it's a tool to hold in reserve if stock is still excess closer to expiry.
questions.concept: Inventory reduction / responding to demand decline
questions.consequence: Orders slow. Weeks later, a batch is still sitting on the shelf, closer to its expiry date.

questions.title: A Batch Nearing Expiry
questions.situation: Despite slower ordering, some stock is now approaching expiry faster than normal demand can clear it.
questions.optionA: Discount this batch now to clear it before it expires, accepting a lower margin.
questions.optionB: Try to negotiate a return or exchange of the excess batch with the supplier, even if it takes more effort.
questions.explanation: A negotiated return recovers value that a distress discount simply gives away. It's worth attempting first — discounting remains the fallback if a return isn't possible.
questions.consequence: The supplier agrees to a partial return. The crisis is essentially over — now the relationships need rebuilding.

questions.title: Rebuilding the Old Relationship
questions.situation: The outbreak has passed. The regular supplier, now back to normal capacity, wants Shivam to return to being an exclusive, loyal customer like before.
questions.optionA: Return to sourcing primarily/exclusively from the regular supplier, given years of trust and better base pricing.
questions.optionB: Keep a smaller ongoing order with the new (emergency) supplier too, even at slightly higher cost, to preserve the backup relationship.
questions.explanation: The whole crisis demonstrated what single-sourcing risk actually costs. A modest ongoing order to the backup supplier is cheap insurance against the next disruption — the lesson shouldn't evaporate the moment things feel normal again.
questions.concept: Supply chain resilience / long-term sourcing strategy
questions.consequence: Dual sourcing becomes permanent policy. Attention shifts to what was lost — and learned.

questions.title: Customers Who Never Came Back
questions.situation: Some regular customers who switched to the rival pharmacy during the stockout days still haven't returned.
questions.optionA: Proactively reach out to former customers with reassurance that stock is now reliable.
questions.optionB: Let word-of-mouth about Shivam's crisis performance bring customers back naturally over time.
questions.explanation: Passive reliance on word-of-mouth risks permanent share loss to the competitor who's now familiar to those customers. A direct, low-cost outreach actively recovers the relationship instead of hoping it repairs itself.
questions.consequence: Some customers return. Pricing is the next thing to settle.

questions.title: Normalizing the Price
questions.situation: Procurement costs have returned to pre-crisis levels now that supply lines are stable.
questions.optionA: Reduce prices back to pre-crisis levels immediately, to rebuild goodwill.
questions.optionB: Keep prices slightly elevated a little longer to recover the margin lost during the crisis.
questions.explanation: Shivam held its price during the crisis specifically on the basis of reliability, not opportunism. Keeping prices elevated now that costs have actually dropped contradicts that stance and risks the trust just rebuilt.
questions.concept: Pricing strategy / consistency in long-term customer trust
questions.consequence: Prices normalize. The bigger question now is what Shivam's sourcing policy should look like going forward — for everything, not just this one item.

questions.title: Setting Policy for All Critical Items
questions.situation: Reflecting on the whole episode, the owner must decide how far to apply the dual-sourcing lesson across the rest of the store's stock.
questions.optionA: Formally adopt dual/multiple sourcing for all critical, high-demand medicines, even though it means managing more supplier relationships.
questions.optionB: Keep single-sourcing as the default for most items, but pre-identify backup suppliers only for a short list of the most critical, high-risk items.
questions.explanation: Blanket dual-sourcing across every product sounds like the "safe" lesson to take away, but for a single-outlet pharmacy it creates coordination cost far beyond the benefit. Resilience should be proportionate to risk — concentrated where a stockout would actually be damaging.
questions.concept: Proportionate risk management / resilience vs. complexity
questions.consequence: Policy is set for critical items only. One more capability gap remains from the crisis.

questions.title: Investing in Better Information
questions.situation: Throughout the crisis, faster and better information (sales data, supplier stock signals) repeatedly helped Shivam make better calls. The owner now considers investing in a basic digital inventory/sales tracking system.
questions.optionA: Invest in a basic digital tracking system now, despite the cost and the staff time needed to learn it.
questions.optionB: Stick with the manual/paper system that's worked for years, since the crisis is over and the cost can be avoided.
questions.explanation: Nearly every good decision in this game — moderated forecasting, dynamic reorder points, catching the hospital's panic order, information sharing with the supplier — depended on having decent information. That's a durable capability worth investing in, not a one-time crisis expense.
questions.concept: Information systems / technology as a logistics enabler
questions.consequence: The system is adopted. One final decision remains — the overall philosophy going forward.

questions.title: The Long-Term Philosophy
questions.situation: Shivam now has: a dual-sourcing policy for critical items, a recovering customer base, a new tracking system, and hard-won lessons about safety stock and forecasting. The owner must decide the operating philosophy going forward.
questions.optionA: Prioritize returning to a lean, low-cost operation now that things are stable, since resilience has an ongoing cost.
questions.optionB: Accept slightly higher ongoing costs — dual sourcing, better information systems, some extra safety stock on critical items — as a permanent trade-off for a more resilient supply chain.
questions.explanation: This is the crisis's central lesson. Pure cost-minimization is exactly what left Shivam exposed at the start of this story. The modest ongoing cost of preparedness is small next to the cost of waiting — a stockout, a lost hospital contract, customers who don't come back. A resilient supply chain isn't the cheapest one; it's the one that survives the next shock.
questions.consequence: Game ends — Shivam has built a genuinely more resilient supply chain than the one it started with.
